memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "'He is to wring its head from its neck, not dividing it completely, and is to splash some of the blood of the sin offering against the side of the altar; the rest of the blood must be drained out at the base of the altar. It is a sin offering.'" - Lev 5:8b-9 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
There is no way to make this verse pleasant. The bird's neck is wrung. Blood is splashed on the altar. The rest drains into the ground.

Leviticus refuses to be tasteful about sin.

We live in a culture — and often in churches — that prefers its religion clean. We speak of "mistakes," "brokenness," "struggles," "issues." All of those words have their place. But Scripture also insists on a vocabulary that makes us uncomfortable, because comfort was never the goal.

Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness (Heb 9:22). That sentence is not a leftover from a primitive age. It is the logic of the cross.

If we lose the offensiveness of sin, we lose the wonder of the cross. A God who simply overlooks wrongdoing needs no crucifixion. It is precisely because sin is this serious that Golgotha was necessary.

And then look at the last four words of the verse: It is a sin offering. Not "it is a punishment." Not "it is a penalty you deserved." An offering — something given, something provided, something that stands in your place.

The blood on that altar was never yours. That is the mercy in it.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Have I softened my language about sin until the cross no longer seems necessary?
2. When did I last let myself feel the weight of what my forgiveness cost?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Lord, keep me from making sin comfortable. Let the cost of the cross break through my familiarity with it. Amen.
